question: Since 2021, Polish company Control Process S.A. has been carrying out a contract worth over EUR 36 million to construct a mechanical biological treatment plant for municipal waste in Lviv. In March 2026, the Lviv authorities unilaterally terminated the contract even though the investment was around 95 % complete.

The company won all FIDIC arbitration proceedings and obtained a ruling from the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in Paris on 16 May 2026 confirming the unlawfulness of the Ukrainian side’s actions.

Despite these arbitration decisions, the Lviv authorities are continuing to refuse to pay what the company is owed, estimated to be around EUR 17-18 million, and are failing to implement binding arbitration decisions and stopping representatives of the company and the Polish Consulate General from accessing the investment site. 1.

Will the Commission, in assessing Ukraine's compliance with the rule of law and foreign investment protection standards as part of the accession process, take into account cases in which local authorities fail to enforce binding arbitration awards against EU investors, including the case of Control Process S.A. and the ICC ruling of 16 May 2026?

How is the Commission monitoring Ukraine’s compliance with foreign investment protection standards and the principles of the rule of law and legal certainty in the context of the accession process, in particular as regards the enforcement of binding arbitration decisions?

What action does the Commission intend to take to ensure that EU funds for the reconstruction of Ukraine do not reach public or municipal entities that do not implement final and binding arbitration decisions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The Commission follows closely the capacity of the Ukrainian authorities to ensure effective remedies and legal certainty, including the effective protection of investors’ rights.

While the Commission cannot comment on individual cases and court proceedings, it takes systemic issues into account in its regular monitoring and assessment of Ukraine’s EU accessionrelated reforms. Information on delays or irregularities in individual cases may be relevant where they point to wider structural shortcomings.

The Commission supports the strengthening of legal certainty for EU businesses active or investing in Ukraine by leveraging its financial conditionality, technical support and regular engagement with the Ukrainian authorities. Support under the Ukraine Facility links disbursements to the implementation of agreed reform steps, including in the areas of rule of law and business environment.

The Commission further supports measures aimed at improving the investment climate, promoting transparent and predictable regulation, and reinforcing safeguards for property rights, contract enforcement and dispute resolution. The Commission will continue monitoring developments in these areas, while consistently underlining the importance of a stable and predictable legal framework for economic operators.
